idiom_name: closure-passing mediator (withRecord(req) { record => ... }) over private members
implementation_notes: The classic guard object becomes either a private member plus one mediating method or, more idiomatically, a closure-passing mediator that never lets the resource reference escape: withRecord(subject, id) { record => ... } runs the policy check and only then applies the caller's function, so there is no window in which an unchecked reference is held. Scala's private and private[scope] qualifiers (members are public by default; private hides them from outside the class) provide the intra-process part, and the JVM caveats of Java apply: reflection can reach private members and no security manager enforces this for you any more. Immutability helps - a case class whose fields are private to the mediator cannot be mutated behind the check, only copied - but it does not confine a copy that has been handed out.
pitfalls: An implicit or given Store (or an implicit conversion from the guard) in scope lets callers reach the resource directly; keep the backing store private and un-implicited.
Immutability is not confinement: a case class copied out of the mediator is an unmediated reference, so return only what the caller may keep.
private and private[scope] are JVM-level and reflection (setAccessible) can bypass them; in-process mediation here is for trusted code.
Custom extractors or unapply on the protected type can expose internals; the mediator's API should not return an extractor over the raw resource.
